title: DOE Seeks Input on Cryogenic and Quantum Supercomputing Testbeds
html:
Insider Brief

  • The U.S. Department of Energy is seeking input on potential testbeds for cryogenic technologies and the integration of quantum computing with classical high-performance computing.
  • DOE is asking researchers and suppliers to identify technical requirements, scalable infrastructure designs, estimated costs and potential partnership models.
  • Responses are due Dec. 17, 2026, and will inform planning without committing DOE to funding or a contract competition.
  • Image: U.S. Department of Energy seal (DOE)

Building a useful quantum computer will likely mean building systems around it — systems that rely on classical computing resources that help it operate and the connections that allow them to work together.

The U.S. Department of Energy gets it.

The department is seeking industry and research input on two interconnected testbed initiatives intended to help developers advance cryogenic technologies and integrate quantum computers with classical high-performance computing systems.

The recently issued request for information asks potential users and suppliers to describe the equipment, computing resources and partnerships needed to support the proposed infrastructure. Responses are due Dec. 17th of this year.

Ultimately, the effort would guide planning for a national resource that gives researchers access to equipment and instrumentation that could otherwise be too expensive to acquire or too burdensome to maintain. Its scope includes quantum computing, sensing, classical electronics operating at cryogenic temperatures and the integration of quantum processors with conventional computing systems.

The document is a request for information, rather than a request for proposals. In other words, the DOE is gathering ideas and technical information to help shape the potential testbeds, rather than asking organizations to compete for a contract. Responses are voluntary and will inform planning and possible future funding opportunities. The request does not commit the department to funding the facilities or holding a competition.

DOE’s Advanced Scientific Computing Research program, within the Office of Science, is seeking feedback from businesses of all sizes, universities, national laboratories and other research organizations. It also wants to hear from suppliers interested in designing, building or helping operate the potential facilities.

Cooling Infrastructure That Can Grow

The cryogenic initiative would support work on quantum technologies and classical computing components that require extremely low operating temperatures.

DOE is asking prospective users to specify their temperature and cooling requirements, the equipment they would need and the connections required between cold devices and room-temperature systems. Researchers are also asked to explain how their needs could evolve over the next five to 10 years.

A central question is how the infrastructure could help researchers connect quantum processing units with classical computing logic. The department wants technical requirements that address both current technologies and more demanding future systems.

For suppliers, the request emphasizes two capabilities: accommodating different experimental technologies and expanding economically over time. DOE says an approach addressing only one of those needs would be insufficient.

Potential configurations include helium-4 cooling systems, dilution refrigerators using helium-3 and helium-4 mixtures and combinations of cooling technologies.

DOE is requesting rough costs and deployment timelines for infrastructure capable of supporting two or four progressively scaled experimental systems, alongside approximately 10 to 40 smaller experiments. Suppliers are asked to identify facility requirements such as electrical power, cooling water, floor space and crane support, as well as maintenance and spare-parts needs.

The department places particular emphasis on keeping experiments running. The request says reliability and flexibility should take priority over the overall thermal efficiency of the combined cooling infrastructure, reflecting the proposed facility’s role in supporting varied research activities.

Connecting Quantum and Classical Systems

The second initiative would focus on integrating quantum computing with high-performance computing resources, including work supporting fault-tolerant quantum computing.

DOE wants users to identify research that such a testbed could advance, including algorithm and application development, error correction and improvements to computing systems.

Respondents are asked to describe how quickly information must move between quantum and classical systems and how much data those connections must carry. They should also identify required computing resources, software and access arrangements, including whether they would bring their own hardware.

Suppliers are asked which qubit technologies their proposed architectures could support and how the infrastructure would grow as quantum systems scale.

The request also covers software for scheduling work and managing resources across quantum and classical machines. Vendors should describe staffing needs, potential national laboratory involvement and arrangements for intellectual property generated through joint work or technology integration.

An accompanying security appendix sets out provisions concerning foreign influence, ownership changes, investments, technology transfers and equipment access. DOE is inviting optional feedback on those terms, including alternative wording intended to support the prompt establishment of partnerships.

Responses are limited to 10 pages, including attachments and cover letters, excluding the optional security appendix. Submissions should be emailed to [email protected] with “Cryogenic and Quantum High-Performance Computing Testbed” in the subject line.

Matt Swayne

MENTIONED IN THE ARTICLE

The mission of the Department of Energy is to ensure America's security and prosperity by addressing its energy, environmental, and nuclear challenges through transformative science and technology solutions. In September, 2022, Research supported by ASCR demonstrated that classical machine learning algorithms can accurately predict ground state properties and classify quantum phases of matter using data generated from quantum experiments. In November, 2022, Research supported by Q-NEXT revealed that the performance of a sensor network is constrained by the intrinsic noise associated with the quantum states used in the network. In March, 2023, Research funded by DOE SC NP achieved the first experimental observation of entanglement between dissimilar particles, specifically positive and negative pions. In August, 2023, Research funded by DOE SC BER demonstrated strong preservation of entanglement in a two-photon absorption process involving organic molecules, offering a new approach for developing quantum light-based spectroscopy and microscopy.
